html:
A user signs up, and your app must create the account, send a welcome email, resize their photo and update analytics. If the sign-up request does all of that, it's slow, and it fails when the email service is down. A message queue lets the request do the essential part and hand the rest off.

What a Queue Does

A producer puts a message on a queue. A consumer takes it off and does the work, later and separately.

sign-up ──► [ queue: "user-created" ] ──► email worker
                                     └──► photo worker

That gives you:

  • Faster responses: the sign-up answers as soon as the account exists.
  • Resilience: if the email service is down, messages wait in the queue instead of failing the sign-up.
  • Absorbing bursts: a flood of 10,000 orders a minute is processed at the pace the workers can handle.
  • Independent scaling: add more photo workers without touching anything else.

Queues vs Event Streams

There are two main models, and they behave differently.

Message Queues (RabbitMQ, Amazon SQS)

  • A message goes to one consumer and is removed once it's acknowledged.
  • Several workers share the load of one queue.
  • Good for tasks: send this email, resize this image.

Event Streams (Kafka, Amazon Kinesis, Redis Streams)

  • Messages are appended to a log and kept for a set time, like 7 days.
  • Each consumer group reads at its own position (offset), and several groups read the same events independently.
  • A topic is split into partitions; order is kept within a partition, and each partition is read by one consumer of a group.
  • Good for events many systems care about, and for replaying history after a bug fix.
Question Queue (RabbitMQ, SQS) Stream (Kafka)
After reading, the message is Removed Kept, until retention ends
Several kinds of consumers One queue each One topic, many groups
Replay old messages No Yes
Ordering Mostly per queue Per partition

Delivery Guarantees

Networks fail, and consumers crash halfway. So a broker gives one of these promises:

  • At most once: a message may be lost, but never processed twice.
  • At least once: a message is never lost, but may be processed twice, for example if the consumer crashes after doing the work but before acknowledging it.
  • Exactly once: possible within some systems (like Kafka transactions), but across real side effects, such as sending an email, you still end up needing the next point.

Most systems choose at least once, and make consumers idempotent: processing the same message twice has the same effect as once. Store the IDs of processed messages, or make the operation naturally repeatable, like "set status to paid" instead of "add 10 to the balance".

Retries and Dead-Letter Queues

When processing fails:

  1. Retry with a growing delay (exponential backoff), since many failures are temporary.
  2. After a few attempts, move the message to a dead-letter queue (DLQ), so one bad message doesn't block everything behind it.
  3. Alert on the DLQ, fix the cause, and replay the messages.

Ordering

Strict order across a whole system is expensive. Usually you only need order per entity: all events of one order, in sequence. With Kafka, use the order ID as the message key, so all its events land in the same partition, in order.

Backpressure

If producers are faster than consumers, the queue grows. Watch the queue length or consumer lag: growing all the time means you need more consumers, or faster ones. A queue absorbs bursts; it doesn't fix a system that's always too slow.

When Not to Use a Queue

If the user needs the result right away, like "is this password correct?", a queue only adds delay. Queues are for work that can happen a moment later.

The Answer in Short

  1. A queue decouples producers from consumers: faster responses, resilience and burst absorption.
  2. Queues (RabbitMQ, SQS) remove messages once handled; streams (Kafka) keep them and let many groups read and replay.
  3. Most systems deliver at least once, so make consumers idempotent.
  4. Retry with backoff, then send failing messages to a dead-letter queue.
  5. Keep order per entity with a message key, and watch queue length or consumer lag.
